_about: Writings outside the 66 books that the site cites. tier: dc = deuterocanonical (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, the Apocrypha for Protestants, not in the Jewish Bible); orth = Scripture for Orthodox Christians only; eth = Scripture only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church; other = in no Bible today; early = an early Christian writing, in no Bible today; lost = a book the Bible names that has not survived; world = a writing of another people or religion, neither Jewish nor Christian, read on this site from a Christian standpoint (tools/agent-writer-world.md). aka: other names the site may use; a name ending in # matches only before a chapter number ("Judith 9", not Judith the wife of Esau). Never list "2 Esdras": the site uses it for the Greek translation of Ezra-Nehemiah, which is not a separate book; the apocalypse is "4 Ezra". topic: the site topic page about the work, if there is one. book: the site book id once the work has its own pages.

1-enoch.name: 1 Enoch
1-enoch.note: Jude 14–15 quotes it (1 Enoch 1:9), and 1 Peter 3:19–20 and 2 Peter 2:4 may echo its story of the Watchers. Fragments of it in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

greek-ending-of-job.name: Greek ending of Job
greek-ending-of-job.note: The Septuagint's addition after Job 42:17 (Rahlfs 42:17a–e): Job will rise again, and he is identified with Jobab, king of Edom (Genesis 36:33). It is part of the Greek Old Testament read by Orthodox churches; it is not in the Hebrew Bible or the Vulgate.

book-of-jashar.name: Book of Jashar
book-of-jashar.note: Joshua 10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18 quote it. The "Book of Jasher" printed in 1625 and translated into English in 1840 is a medieval Hebrew retelling, not this book.

book-of-the-wars.name: Book of the Wars of the LORD
aka: Book of the Wars of the LORD
scroll of the Wars of the LORD

genesis-apocryphon.name: Genesis Apocryphon
genesis-apocryphon.note: An Aramaic retelling of Genesis found in Qumran Cave 1, copied in the first century BC. It expands the stories of Lamech, Noah and Abraham and shares traditions with 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

book-of-giants.name: Book of Giants
book-of-giants.note: An Aramaic book about the giants born to the Watchers, known from Qumran fragments and later reused by the Manichaeans. It belongs to the Enoch tradition.

damascus-document.name: Damascus Document
damascus-document.note: A rule book of a Jewish sect related to the Qumran community, found in the Cairo Geniza in 1896 and later in Qumran fragments. It cites Jubilees as an authority.

3-enoch.name: 3 Enoch
3-enoch.note: A Hebrew Jewish mystical work from late antiquity or the early Middle Ages, in which Enoch becomes the angel Metatron. It is much later than 1 Enoch.

gospel-of-peter.name: Gospel of Peter
gospel-of-peter.note: A second-century account of the passion and resurrection, known from a fragment found at Akhmim in Egypt in 1886. Bishop Serapion of Antioch rejected it around AD 200.

apocalypse-of-peter.name: Apocalypse of Peter
apocalypse-of-peter.note: A second-century vision of heaven and hell. The Muratorian list (late second century) accepts it but says some would not have it read in church. Its fullest text survives in Ge’ez (classical Ethiopic).

melchizedek-scroll.name: 11QMelchizedek
melchizedek-scroll.note: A fragmentary Hebrew text from Qumran Cave 11, copied in the first century BC. It reads Psalm 82:1–2, Isaiah 61 and Leviticus 25 as prophecies of Melchizedek, a heavenly figure who frees the captives and judges Belial in the last jubilee.

apocryphal-psalms-11q11.name: 11QApocryphal Psalms
apocryphal-psalms-11q11.note: A Hebrew scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (copied about 50 BC to AD 50) of songs for driving out demons, some credited to David and Solomon. It ends with a form of Psalm 91.

copper-scroll.name: Copper Scroll
copper-scroll.note: A list of hidden treasures engraved on copper, found in Qumran Cave 3 in 1952 (first century AD). It appears to name a place Beth Eshdatayin, often linked with the pool of Bethesda (John 5:2).

gospel-of-the-nazarenes.name: Gospel of the Nazarenes
gospel-of-the-nazarenes.note: A lost Jewish-Christian gospel in Aramaic or Syriac, close to Matthew, known only from quotations in Jerome and other church writers (300s–400s). Jerome cites its sayings as from the Gospel "according to the Hebrews"; modern scholars sort the Jewish-Christian gospel fragments into this work, the Gospel of the Hebrews and the Gospel of the Ebionites.

gospel-of-the-ebionites.name: Gospel of the Ebionites
gospel-of-the-ebionites.note: A lost Greek Jewish-Christian gospel (100s), known only from quotations in Epiphanius, Panarion 30; it blends Matthew, Mark and Luke and makes John the Baptist and Jesus vegetarian.

protevangelium-of-james.name: Protevangelium of James
protevangelium-of-james.note: A Greek story of Mary's birth and childhood and of Jesus' birth (about AD 150), the source of the names Joachim and Anna and of the view that Jesus' brothers were Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage.

toledot-yeshu.name: Toledot Yeshu
toledot-yeshu.note: A medieval Jewish counter-story of Jesus' life, in many versions, written in reaction to Christian claims and persecution; it repeats the charge of illegitimacy.

community-rule.name: Community Rule
community-rule.note: The rule book of the community at Qumran, found in Cave 1 in 1947 (copied about 100–75 BC); it applies Isaiah 40:3 to the community's withdrawal into the wilderness.

war-scroll.name: War Scroll
aka: War of the Sons of Light Against the Sons of Darkness
war-scroll.note: A Qumran text, copied in the first century BC, describing the final war between the sons of light and the sons of darkness, with God's angels fighting on the side of the faithful.

gospel-of-the-hebrews.name: Gospel of the Hebrews
gospel-of-the-hebrews.note: A lost Jewish-Christian gospel of the second century, known only from quotations in Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Jerome and others. Scholars disagree on whether these quotations come from one, two or three gospels. Some of the quotations Jerome gives under this name are now usually assigned to the Gospel of the Nazarenes.

4q521.name: Messianic Apocalypse (4Q521)
4q521.note: A fragmentary Hebrew text from Qumran Cave 4 (first century BC) that says heaven and earth will listen to God's anointed and that the Lord will heal the wounded, raise the dead and bring good news to the poor.

didascalia-apostolorum.name: Didascalia Apostolorum
didascalia-apostolorum.note: A church order written in Greek in Syria in the 200s, surviving mainly in Syriac; it tells the story of Jesus and a woman accused of sin (compare John 7:53–8:11) to urge bishops to receive repentant sinners.

book-of-mormon.name: Book of Mormon
book-of-mormon.note: Scripture, alongside the Bible, for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and other churches of the Latter Day Saint movement (such as Community of Christ), published by Joseph Smith in 1830; in 3 Nephi 15:21 the risen Jesus tells people in the Americas that they are the "other sheep" of John 10:16. It is not part of any Bible.

gospel-of-judas.name: Gospel of Judas
gospel-of-judas.note: A Gnostic gospel of the 100s, known to Irenaeus and found in a Coptic copy of about AD 300, published in 2006, in which Judas alone understands Jesus.

acts-of-pilate.name: Acts of Pilate
acts-of-pilate.note: A Greek account of Jesus's trial, death and descent to the dead (400s in its present form), later part of the Gospel of Nicodemus; it presents Pilate favorably.

acts-of-peter.name: Acts of Peter
acts-of-peter.note: A Greek story of Peter's preaching and contests in Rome (late 100s), known mainly from a Latin manuscript at Vercelli; its account of his martyrdom also survives in Greek. It tells of the "Quo vadis?" meeting and of Peter crucified head downward at his own request.

gospel-of-mary.name: Gospel of Mary
gospel-of-mary.note: A second-century Christian writing, surviving in fragments in Coptic (the Berlin Codex) and Greek, in which Mary Magdalene teaches the disciples what the risen Savior revealed to her and Peter disputes her authority.

gospel-of-philip.name: Gospel of Philip
gospel-of-philip.note: A third-century collection of Gnostic sayings in Coptic, found at Nag Hammadi in 1945, which calls Mary Magdalene Jesus' "companion" and says he often kissed her; the text is damaged at that point.

ascension-of-isaiah.name: Ascension of Isaiah
ascension-of-isaiah.note: A Christian writing of the late first or early second century AD, perhaps built on an older Jewish story, preserved complete only in Ge'ez. Chapters 1–5 tell how King Manasseh had Isaiah sawn in two; chapters 6–11 describe Isaiah's journey through the seven heavens and his vision of the Beloved's descent and return.

lives-of-the-prophets.name: Lives of the Prophets
lives-of-the-prophets.note: Short Jewish accounts of the prophets' origins, deaths and burial places, probably first century AD, preserved in Greek in Christian copies. It says Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh and buried near Siloam.

gospel-of-pseudo-matthew.name: Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew
gospel-of-pseudo-matthew.note: A Latin retelling of the birth and childhood of Mary and Jesus, probably from the 600s AD, drawn largely from the Protevangelium of James. Its chapter 14 places an ox and a donkey at the manger, citing Isaiah 1:3 and Habakkuk 3:2.

isaiah-pesher-4q161.name: Isaiah Pesher (4Q161)
isaiah-pesher-4q161.note: A Qumran commentary on Isaiah 10–11, copied in the late first century BC. It reads the march of 10:28–34 as the last war against the Kittim and the shoot of 11:1–5 as the Branch of David who will rule at the end of days.

sefer-ha-milhamah.name: Sefer ha-Milhamah (4Q285)
sefer-ha-milhamah.note: A Qumran fragment, probably part of a War Rule, from the late first century BC or early first century AD. It quotes Isaiah 10:34–11:1 and tells of the Branch of David, the Prince of the Congregation, and the killing of the enemy's leader.

rule-of-the-blessings.name: Rule of the Blessings (1QSb)
rule-of-the-blessings.note: Blessings for the end of days, copied on the same scroll as the Qumran Community Rule (about 100 BC). Its blessing of the Prince of the Congregation draws on Isaiah 11:2–5.

isaiah-pesher-4q164.name: Isaiah Pesher (4Q164)
isaiah-pesher-4q164.note: A small Qumran commentary on Isaiah 54:11–12, copied in the first century BC. It reads the jewels of the rebuilt city as the community: its foundation stones are the priests and the people who laid the foundation of the council of the community, and its battlements are the twelve chief priests.

songs-of-the-sage.name: Songs of the Sage (4Q510–511)
songs-of-the-sage.note: Hymns from Qumran Cave 4, from the first century BC, in which the Instructor praises God's majesty to frighten off evil spirits. They list "liliths" among the demons, the plural that the Great Isaiah Scroll has at Isaiah 34:14.

alphabet-of-ben-sira.name: Alphabet of Ben Sira
alphabet-of-ben-sira.note: A satirical Hebrew work of the early Middle Ages (probably 800s–1000s AD) with tales about Ben Sira. It contains the earliest known form of the legend that Lilith was Adam's first wife, a story not found in Isaiah 34:14.

life-of-adam-and-eve.name: Life of Adam and Eve
life-of-adam-and-eve.note: A Jewish retelling of the lives of Adam and Eve after Eden, probably from the first centuries AD, preserved in Latin (the Vita), Greek (the Apocalypse of Moses) and other versions. In the Latin, chapters 12–16 tell how the devil refused to worship the image of God in Adam and boasted that he would set his seat above the stars and be like the Most High.

apocalypse-of-elijah.name: Apocalypse of Elijah
apocalypse-of-elijah.note: A Christian apocalypse of the third or fourth century AD, perhaps reworking Jewish material, preserved in Coptic and in a Greek fragment. Origen said Paul's saying in 1 Corinthians 2:9 came from 'the Secrets of Elijah the prophet'; that writing is lost, and the surviving Coptic Apocalypse of Elijah does not contain the saying.

secret-gospel-of-mark.name: Secret Gospel of Mark
secret-gospel-of-mark.note: Disputed: if genuine, an early Christian writing; many scholars judge it a modern forgery. Known only from a letter ascribed to Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200), which Morton Smith said he found in 1958, copied by hand into the back of a printed book at the Mar Saba monastery near Jerusalem. The letter quotes a longer, 'more spiritual' Gospel of Mark used in Alexandria, including a story of a young man raised from the dead and taught at night. The pages are now lost; Smith's black-and-white photographs and colour photographs taken in 1977 survive. It is in no church's Bible.

diatessaron.name: Diatessaron
diatessaron.note: Tatian's harmony of the four Gospels woven into one story (about AD 170), widely read in the Syriac-speaking churches until the 400s. It survives only in later translations and quotations, such as Ephrem the Syrian's commentary.

temple-scroll.name: Temple Scroll
temple-scroll.note: A long Hebrew scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (copied about the turn of the era) that rewrites the laws of the Torah as God's own words about the temple, the festivals and the land. Column 64 applies the law of hanging on a tree (Deuteronomy 21:22–23) to traitors hung alive, which shows that Jews before Jesus linked that law with crucifixion.

nahum-pesher.name: Nahum Pesher (4Q169)
nahum-pesher.note: A Qumran commentary on Nahum, copied in the first century BC. It speaks of a 'Lion of Wrath' who hanged men alive, usually taken as the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus crucifying his Pharisee opponents.

testimonia-4q175.name: Testimonia (4Q175)
testimonia-4q175.note: A single Qumran sheet (about 100–75 BC) that strings together Scripture passages about the figures the community awaited, beginning with the prophet like Moses of Deuteronomy 18:18–19.

pseudo-clementine-recognitions.name: Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions
pseudo-clementine-recognitions.note: A Christian novel about Clement of Rome and the apostle Peter, written in the 200s–300s from older Jewish-Christian sources and preserved in Latin and Syriac. Book 1 makes Gamaliel a secret believer. It is in no church's Bible.

florilegium-4q174.name: Florilegium (4Q174)
florilegium-4q174.note: A Qumran collection of Scripture passages with comments on the last days (copied in the first century BC). It reads Nathan's promise (2 Samuel 7) and Amos 9:11, 'the fallen booth of David,' of the Branch of David who will arise at the end of days, the same verse James quotes in Acts 15:16.

pseudo-dionysius.name: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
pseudo-dionysius.note: Greek writings on the divine names, mystical theology and the heavenly and church hierarchies, written about AD 500 by an unknown Christian influenced by Neoplatonism, under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's convert in Acts 17:34. Highly influential in the medieval East and West; in no church's Bible.

prayer-of-nabonidus.name: Prayer of Nabonidus
prayer-of-nabonidus.note: A fragmentary Aramaic text from Qumran Cave 4 (4Q242), copied about 75–50 BC, in which the Babylonian king Nabonidus tells how he was struck with an illness for seven years in Teman until a Jewish diviner forgave his sin and told him to honor the Most High God. It is often compared with Daniel 4.

pesher-habakkuk.name: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab)
pesher-habakkuk.note: A commentary on Habakkuk 1–2 from Qumran Cave 1, copied in the late first century BC. It applies the prophet's words line by line to the community's own history: the Teacher of Righteousness, the Wicked Priest, the Man of the Lie and the Kittim (probably the Romans). At Habakkuk 1:5 it reads "the traitors," close to the Greek "scoffers" that Paul quotes in Acts 13:41.

acts-of-paul.name: Acts of Paul
acts-of-paul.note: A Greek story of Paul's travels and martyrdom written in Asia Minor in the late 100s; Tertullian says a presbyter wrote it out of love for Paul and was removed from office. Its best-known part tells of Thecla, a young woman of Iconium who left her betrothed to follow Paul, and it gives the only ancient description of Paul's appearance. It is in no church's Bible.

aramaic-apocalypse-4q246.name: Aramaic Apocalypse (4Q246)
aramaic-apocalypse-4q246.note: A damaged Aramaic fragment from Qumran Cave 4, copied in the late first century BC. It speaks of one who "will be called son of God, and they will call him son of the Most High," and of a kingdom that lasts forever, wording very close to Luke 1:32–35. Scholars debate whether this figure is a coming savior-king or an arrogant ruler who claims divine titles.

letter-of-aristeas.name: Letter of Aristeas
letter-of-aristeas.note: A Greek Jewish writing, probably from Alexandria in the 100s BC, that tells how seventy-two elders, six from each tribe of Israel, translated the Law of Moses into Greek for Ptolemy II of Egypt. The story it tells is the source of the name Septuagint (the Seventy): later tradition rounded its seventy-two translators to seventy. It is in no church's Bible.

gospel-of-the-egyptians.name: Gospel of the Egyptians
gospel-of-the-egyptians.note: A lost Greek gospel of the 100s, known only from quotations in Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 3), in which Salome questions Jesus about death and marriage. It is in no church's Bible. It is a different work from the Coptic "Gospel of the Egyptians" found at Nag Hammadi.

muratorian-fragment.name: Muratorian Fragment
muratorian-fragment.note: A Latin list of the books read in the church, with comments on each, found in an eighth-century manuscript in Milan and published by L. A. Muratori in 1740. Its beginning is lost. Most scholars date the Greek original to the late 100s, in or near Rome; some (Sundberg, Hahneman) argue for the 300s in the East. It names Luke as the author of Acts and says Luke left out Peter's death and Paul's journey to Spain. It is in no church's Bible; it is a witness to which books were read.

rule-of-the-congregation.name: Rule of the Congregation (1QSa)
rule-of-the-congregation.note: A short rule for "the whole congregation of Israel in the last days," copied on the same scroll as the Qumran Community Rule (about 100 BC). It bars people with physical defects from the assembly because angels are present, and describes a communal meal at which the Messiah of Israel is present.

infancy-gospel-of-thomas.name: Infancy Gospel of Thomas
infancy-gospel-of-thomas.note: A Greek collection of stories about Jesus between the ages of five and twelve, probably from the second century, unrelated to the sayings Gospel of Thomas. The boy Jesus makes clay birds fly, strikes down children who annoy him and silences his teachers; it ends with a version of Luke 2:41–52. It is in no church's Bible, and early writers such as Irenaeus already treated stories of this kind as fictions.

sibylline-oracles.name: Sibylline Oracles
sibylline-oracles.note: Greek oracles in the voice of the Sibyl, the prophetess of Greek legend, collected in twelve or more books. Books 3 to 5 are mostly Jewish (from about 150 BC to the early 100s AD) and call Rome a wicked power and Nero a matricide who will return from beyond the Euphrates; other books are Christian reworkings. Early Christian writers quoted them, but no church counts them as Scripture.

apocalypse-of-abraham.name: Apocalypse of Abraham
apocalypse-of-abraham.note: A Jewish apocalypse from soon after AD 70, preserved only in Old Church Slavonic. Abraham turns from his father's idols, is taken up to see God's fiery throne with living creatures around it, and is shown history up to the temple's fall. In no Bible.

martyrdom-of-polycarp.name: Martyrdom of Polycarp
martyrdom-of-polycarp.note: A letter from the church at Smyrna telling how its bishop Polycarp was burned in the stadium, about AD 155 to 160. It is the oldest account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament. In no Bible.

thanksgiving-hymns.name: Thanksgiving Hymns (1QH)
thanksgiving-hymns.note: A scroll of hymns from Qumran Cave 1 (copied in the first century BC), most beginning "I thank you, Lord." The singer praises God for rescue from the pit and from the powers of Belial. In no Bible.

new-jerusalem-text.name: New Jerusalem text (Qumran)
new-jerusalem-text.note: An Aramaic work found in pieces in several Qumran caves (copied in the first century BC and first century AD). An angel guide measures a huge future Jerusalem, its gates named for the twelve tribes, its streets and houses, with a measuring rod, much as in Ezekiel 40 to 48 and Revelation 21. In no Bible.

epistle-to-the-laodiceans.name: Epistle to the Laodiceans
epistle-to-the-laodiceans.note: A short Latin letter claiming to be the letter Paul mentions in Colossians 4:16, stitched together mostly from phrases of Philippians. It is known from about the 500s, was copied into many Latin Bibles in the Middle Ages, and is now judged a forgery. No church counts it as Scripture today. Paul's real letter to Laodicea is lost.

letters-of-ignatius.name: Letters of Ignatius
aka: Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians
letters-of-ignatius.note: Seven letters written by Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, about AD 110 while he was being taken to Rome to die: to the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia and Smyrna, and to Polycarp. They are among the earliest Christian writings after the New Testament. In no Bible.

mmt-4q394.name: Some of the Works of the Torah (4QMMT)
mmt-4q394.note: A letter or treatise from Qumran Cave 4 (copied in the 100s to 50s BC), listing rules on which its writers, a group that later formed the Qumran community, disagreed with the Jerusalem temple leaders, and urging the reader to follow them. It uses the Hebrew phrase 'some of the works of the Torah' and ends by saying that doing what is right will be reckoned to the reader as righteousness, which scholars (Dunn, Fitzmyer) compare with Paul's 'works of the law' and Genesis 15:6.

pearl-of-great-price.name: Pearl of Great Price
pearl-of-great-price.note: Scripture, alongside the Bible and the Book of Mormon, for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, published in 1851 and including Joseph Smith—History, Joseph Smith's account of his visions and of the gold plates. It is not part of any Bible.

ezekiel-the-tragedian.name: Ezekiel the Tragedian (Exagoge)
ezekiel-the-tragedian.note: A Greek verse drama on the Exodus, written by a Jewish author of that name, probably in Alexandria in the second century BC. About 270 lines survive, quoted by Alexander Polyhistor and preserved by Eusebius (Preparation for the Gospel 9.28-29). Its author is not the prophet Ezekiel. In no Bible.

apocryphon-of-ezekiel.name: Apocryphon of Ezekiel
apocryphon-of-ezekiel.note: A lost work in Ezekiel's name that early Christian writers such as Clement of Alexandria quote, and of which only fragments survive. Some scholars have linked it with the Pseudo-Ezekiel texts from Qumran; the link is not settled. In no Bible.

pseudo-ezekiel.name: Pseudo-Ezekiel (Qumran)
pseudo-ezekiel.note: Fragments in several copies from Qumran Cave 4 (4Q385-388, 4Q391) that retell visions in Ezekiel's voice, including the dry bones and a vision of the chariot, with additions of their own. They were copied in the first century BC. In no Bible.

paralipomena-of-jeremiah.name: 4 Baruch
aka: Rest of the Words of Baruch
paralipomena-of-jeremiah.note: A Jewish story about the fall of Jerusalem and the exile, in the names of Jeremiah and Baruch, probably written in the early 100s AD with Christian additions. It tells how Jeremiah sent Baruch away, and how Abimelech slept for sixty-six years. It survives in Greek, Ethiopic and other languages. It is Scripture only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which calls it the Rest of the Words of Baruch; it is in no Catholic, other Orthodox or Protestant Bible.

jannes-and-jambres-book.name: Jannes and Jambres
jannes-and-jambres-book.note: A Jewish book about Pharaoh's two magicians. Origen says there was an apocryphal book of this name; Greek fragments survive in the Chester Beatty Papyri (no. XVI, edited by Albert Pietersma), and an Ethiopic fragment was found in 2014. Not Scripture in any church. It shows how Jewish storytellers expanded Exodus 7, and gives no independent knowledge of the magicians. The names appear in 2 Timothy 3:8, the Damascus Document, Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and the Talmud.

atrahasis.name: Atrahasis
atrahasis.note: A Babylonian poem in three tablets that runs from the making of humankind to the Flood. Its hero, Atrahasis, survives the Flood in a boat.

epic-of-gilgamesh.name: Epic of Gilgamesh
epic-of-gilgamesh.note: The Babylonian poem about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and his search for life without death. Its Tablet XI tells the Flood story, close to Atrahasis.

enuma-elish.name: Enuma Elish
enuma-elish.note: The Babylonian creation poem, which praises the god Marduk.
